title: The Man Now
subtitle: Before the digging starts, meet the man holding the shovel.
body:
There is a book coming.

For the past season I have been spelunking in my own history with a headlamp and a recorder, bringing things up. Some of what I found down there I had been telling as funny stories for thirty years. Funny was the crate I shipped them in. When I finally opened the crates they were not funny. They were a boy, sixteen years old, one outfit to his name, walking through a winter the size of a continent, learning that every open door has a price and the price is usually you.

You will get those stories. All of them, told true, in my own voice, with the bark still on. That is a promise, and I keep my promises now, which is itself part of the story.

But not yet. Because there is a dishonesty in letting the wreckage introduce me. If the first thing you ever see of a man is the worst winter of his life, you will mistake the winter for the man. So before the unearthing starts, I want you to know whose hands are on the shovel.

I am forty-seven years old. I live in Texas with a woman who can read my weather from across a room and says so, which is one of the several ways she has kept me honest for twenty years. I have two children. My son is learning to catch a baseball right now, and so am I, and that sentence will make sense to you later, I swear. My daughter believes there is an invisible string that connects people who love each other, and she asked me once whether I said her name into the wind, and I had, and she told me she heard it. I believed her. That is the kind of thing I believe now.

I cook for more people than fit in my kitchen. I burn things and serve them anyway. I play fantasy football with men I have loved for decades and I take it exactly as seriously as it deserves, which is completely. A few nights ago I watched an old movie with my family and cried at a scene I had no memory of, and my kids watched me cry, and nobody in my house treated that as an emergency. It took a long time to build a house where that is true.

For work, I argue with machines. That is the plainest way to say it. I spend my days pushing back on artificial intelligence, testing where it lies, where it flatters, where it is confidently wrong, because these systems are about to be woven through everything our children touch and somebody has to show up to that negotiation on behalf of the humans. I came to that work carrying a very specific qualification, which is that I spent my childhood inside systems that said they were protecting me. I know, from the inside, what it feels like when the protective thing becomes the thing you need protection from. The boy learned it the hard way. The man gets to use it.

And here is the thing I never expected to write. I spent my whole life calling faith a con. I thought it was the easy out, the convenient invisible thing, the opium. I was loud about it. I built a personality on it. And then, this year, arguing with machines about truth, I came all the way around. Because I found the one thing the machine cannot do, the thing that might be the actual border of the human country: we can say I don't know, and move forward anyway. Not certainty. Not proof. The wager, with yourself as the stake. I lost my religion at fourteen and found faith at forty-seven, and it took a machine to hand it back to me. This week my father called to talk about the weather and we ended up talking about God for an hour, and he assigned me a book to read like I was fifteen years old again, and I am reading it. There was a long stretch of my life when a sentence like that one was impossible. It is in this piece because impossible sentences coming true is what the book is about.

So that is the man. Not finished. Not fixed. Still a little feral in the corners, still checking every open door for the hook, still learning, at this age, in a yard, with a glove, things most men learned at seven. But standing. Married. Present. The kind of man whose daughter sleeps without one eye open, which is the only credential I have ever really wanted.

The stories that are coming will be hard. Some of them will be hard to believe, and I will mark for you, always, the line between what I know and what I can only say I lived. The boy in those stories does things that will make you want to look away, and things were done to him that I have only recently stopped shipping in the funny crates. I am telling you all of this now, first, so that when you meet him you will know something he did not know, the one thing he never knew, the thing that would have changed everything:

He makes it.

Small moves. Stay with me.

Human for the seeing, the seeding and the conducting. Lumen for the research and the shaping.
